sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element (primary buttons, links, cards, section headings, error states) look the same everywhere it appears?** No, the topic icons break the pattern.
   - **Where:** Six of the eight topic cards use thin navy line icons: lightning, key, box, plug, bell and life ring. Two cards use full-colour filled pictures instead. One is the blue and orange credit card on "Billing and invoices" (about x 673–711, y 420–448). The other is the green shield with a check on "Privacy and security" (about x 91–123, y 603–641).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** On a page that is otherwise navy, grey and white, these two are the only saturated colour. The eye jumps to Billing and Privacy before it reads the grid in order, which makes those two topics look more important or featured, but nothing else on the page says they are. The two icons also look like they came from a different icon set or an emoji pack, so the grid looks put together from parts rather than built as one system. That weakens the calm, trustworthy feel a help centre needs.
   - **Why:** Elements of one kind share one style, and a variant appears only where the rules call for it (Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*, introduction). Elements doing the same job should share one colour (Apple Human Interface Guidelines, "Color"; Material Design 3, Color roles). The same component style should mean the same thing everywhere (Nielsen, heuristic 4).
   - **Fix:** Redraw the card and shield as line icons in the same navy, stroke weight and size as the other six, so all eight cards weigh the same. If Billing or Privacy really should stand out, give that a deliberate signal used across the whole grid, not an accident of icon source.
   - **Kind:** Defect (it suggests a priority that isn't there). Weight: minor. The page still does its job (search, or pick a topic), but this is the one thing that breaks its unity.

**What's working.**
- **Headline, subline and search work together.** "How can we help?", the subline "Browse a topic or search the guides." and the wide search field (360–920 px) say what the page is for and offer both ways in within the first second. A first-time viewer can say what this page is for without effort.
- **The topic copy is concrete and finished.** Each card's title is plain and its one-line description says what you'll do or find there ("Track a delivery or start a return.", "Fix sync problems and error messages."). Labels aren't left as bare category names, so a user can match their problem to a card without guessing.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (each kind of element looks the same everywhere it appears).

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** The answer is no. Under the headline, three bold, dark text sizes sit only about 2 px apart:
   - the "Harbor Help Center" wordmark, about 20 px (64,31);
   - the section heading "Browse by topic", about 18 px (64,361);
   - the eight card titles such as "Getting started" and "Billing and invoices", about 16 px semibold (87,486 and so on).

   The section heading and the card titles share the same colour, the same near-black and nearly the same weight. So "Browse by topic" reads as a ninth label, not as the heading over the grid. What sets it apart is its position outside the cards, not its type. The wordmark also blurs into the same band. The result is a page with two clear levels (headline, then everything else) where three were wanted.
   - Why: Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8. A difference must be obvious at a glance, and a size one step larger looks like an accident. Bringhurst, *Elements of Typographic Style* §3.1.1, says to use a modest set of distinct intervals.
   - Fix: make the section heading clearly its own level. Either a clear step up in size (e.g. 22–24 px) or a change of form, such as the headline's serif or a small uppercase grey label. Keep the card titles where they are.
   - Convention. Weight: minor. The card frames already group the titles, so nobody gets lost, but the page has one less level than it needs.

**What's working.**
- The headline dominates without a fight. "How can we help?" is the largest type on the page, the only serif and the only white-on-navy text. It sits in the one dark band, with the search field right under it, so the eye starts in the right place and goes straight to the main action.
- Card titles and descriptions differ in more than size. The titles are near-black semibold and the descriptions are a lighter grey regular. A scanner can read only the titles down the grid.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** None for this section. The full-colour card and shield icons (≈693,433 and ≈107,621) pull the eye ahead of the outlined icons and lift two topics for no reason. That belongs to the pictures and colour sections, not to this one.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (levels of text distinct at a glance)

**Walk (working notes).** I couldn't run the crop script because Bash is not allowed here. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

First read: the eye lands on "How can we help?" in the navy band, then drops to the subtitle and the search field, then to "Browse by topic" and the grid of eight cards. It reads as a calm, tidy help-center landing page. Job (assumed): help a customer find the right help topic or article quickly.

Arrangement and space:
- One grid: yes. There are four card columns at about x 64, 357, 650 and 943, each about 272 wide. Column gaps and row gaps are about 21. Margins are 64 on both sides and match the logo and nav edges.
- Exact alignment, no near-misses: no. The search field (x≈360–920) is a few pixels off the inner card edges below it (x≈357 and ≈922).
- Baselines across columns: yes.
- Space inside groups smaller than between groups: yes.
- One group per box: yes.
- Only related things look alike: yes. The mixed icon styles belong to another section.
- Nothing touching or overlapping: yes.
- Margin from page edge: yes.
- White space gathered: yes.
- Balance: yes.
- Centering has a reason: yes. The single search field is the main action.
- Proportional divisions: yes.
- Eye path: yes.

---

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?**
   - **Where:** The search field in the hero spans about x 360–920. The inner edges of the second and third card columns below it are at about x 357 and x 922. Its edges miss those column lines by roughly 2–3 px.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** Most people won't notice it consciously. The navy band and the heading sit between the field and the cards, which hides the gap. But the field is the one centered element that is nearly as wide as the middle two columns. A careful eye scanning down the page sees it as almost lined up with the grid, which looks like a slip rather than a choice.
   - **Why:** A near-miss reads as an error, while a clear offset reads as intent (layout.md "Break the grid decisively or not at all"). I couldn't open the entry or crop the image, so these numbers are by eye. Check the field's real box against the card columns in the live page.
   - **Fix direction:** Make the search field exactly as wide as the middle two columns plus the gap between them (357–922). Or make it clearly narrower or wider so it doesn't look tied to the grid.
   - **Type:** Convention. **Weight:** minor.

**What's working.**
- **One strict grid sets every edge on the page.** The 64 px side margins are shared by the logo, the "Browse by topic" heading, the first card and the right end of the nav. The cards have matching ~21 px gaps between both columns and rows, and their titles and descriptions sit on the same lines across all four columns. The eight topics read as one even set, and they're quick to scan. Keep the grid when you add or rename topics.
- **The centered hero is centered for a reason.** The heading, subtitle and search field sit on one axis inside a band with wide empty sides. That pulls the eye straight to the one main action, searching. Below it, the grid switches to left alignment for scanning, which is the right split.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (exact alignment or clearly off, no near-misses).

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraphs and columns break cleanly, with no lone short word on a last line?** No. In the topic cards, several two-line descriptions end with one short word alone on the second line. In "Privacy and security", "data." sits alone at about (87, 720). In "Notifications", "where." sits alone at about (673, 720). "receipts." (Billing, about 673, 532), "recovery." (Account, about 380, 532) and "messages." (Troubleshooting, about 966, 720) do the same. Across the grid this gives a row of long first lines with stubs under them. The cards look less even than they should, and the meaning trails off at the end of each blurb. Fix: rewrite the blurbs so they fill both lines more evenly or fit on one line (e.g. "How we protect and store your data" could be shortened, and "Choose which alerts you get" could drop "and where"). Or set the descriptions with balanced wrapping so the two lines come out closer in length. Convention (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.4.2). Weight: minor.

**What's working.** 
- **Two typefaces, each with one job.** The serif display face appears only on "How can we help?", and a single plain sans handles the nav, card titles and descriptions. The headline gets a voice of its own, and the rest of the page stays uniform and easy to scan.
- **Card text is easy to scan.** Each card pairs a bold title of about 16 px with a lighter gray description of about 14 px, and both sit on the same left edge. You can read the titles alone and skip the descriptions.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs and columns break cleanly).

These are judgements by eye from a 1280×800 screenshot with no measured facts file. Sizes and contrast are estimates, and the contrast of the gray descriptions and the search placeholder is close to the 4.5:1 limit, so it's worth checking in a browser. I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was refused, so I worked from the full image, which was small enough for that anyway.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece use a small palette, about one neutral range and one or two hues besides the status colors?** No. The page's color system is navy (header text and hero band, about y 64–312), white, a pale cool gray (page background) and slate line icons. Two of the eight topic icons break it. The Billing and invoices card icon (about x 675–712, y 420–448) is a filled illustration in bright blue, yellow and orange. The Privacy and security icon (about x 92–122, y 603–640) is a filled green shield with a check. Every other icon is a thin slate outline. These two are the only saturated color below the hero, so the eye goes to Billing and Privacy first, though nothing makes them more important than the other six topics. The grid stops reading as a set of equal choices, and the icons look like they came from a different icon set. The orange is also the only warm color on the page, which pulls Billing forward even more. Fix: redraw both as slate outline icons in the same stroke weight as the rest. If you want color in the icons, use one shared accent tint for all eight, not a different picture style for some. Mark: defect (it shifts attention to two topics for no reason and makes the grid look inconsistent), with the mixed icon styles also a matter of taste. Weight: minor. The page still works, but the topic grid looks less finished and less even.

**What's working.**
- **Clear light and dark.** The dark navy hero against the white and pale-gray body gives a strong value split. In grayscale the structure still reads at once: masthead, search band, then the card grid. The white search field on the navy band is the brightest, highest-contrast object above the fold, which suits a help center where searching is the main task.
- **Restrained palette everywhere else.** One navy hue does duty for the brand, headings and hero. The body text and outline icons are muted slate, and the cards are white on a cool gray, so the page feels calm and trustworthy.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (small palette).

**Section.** Pictures: applies. The page has eight topic icons and a text wordmark.

**Findings**
1. **Do the pictures share one rendering style and one level of detail? / Do the icons and line drawings share one stroke weight, cap style, and corner radius?** Two of the eight topic icons come from a different family:
   - The Billing card (about x 673–711, y 420–448) is a detailed, filled, multicolor illustration: a blue card, a yellow chip and an orange dot.
   - The Privacy shield (about x 90–122, y 603–641) is a filled green gradient with a white check.
   - The other six (lightning, key, cube, plug, bell, lifebuoy) are thin navy outline icons with no fill.

   **What the viewer sees:** the two odd icons are the only saturated colors below the hero, so the eye goes to "Billing and invoices" and "Privacy and security" first. That reads as if those topics were promoted, but nothing else on the page says they matter more. The set also looks like it was put together from two icon libraries rather than designed as one. On a support page the topics should be equal, and the false emphasis slows the scan across all eight.

   **Source:** Apple Human Interface Guidelines, "Icons": all interface icons need "a consistent size, level of detail, stroke thickness (or weight), and perspective." The style mismatch itself is common sense.

   **Fix:** redraw or replace the card and shield as simple outline glyphs in the same navy, at the same stroke weight as the other six, so the whole set shares one level of detail. If billing or security really should stand out, do it on purpose through layout or a label, not through a stray icon style.

   Defect. Weight: major. It creates false emphasis in the main browsing grid and is the only thing breaking the set's unity.

**What's working.**
- **The six outline icons** (lightning, key, cube, plug, bell, lifebuoy) look like one family: same navy, same thin stroke, same size, same place in each card. Each one is a plain, familiar metaphor for its topic, so the icons help people scan without needing a second read. Keep this style as the standard the other two follow.
- **The wordmark** "Harbor Help Center" is set as plain navy text with generous clear space in the header. It is simple, recognizable and will hold up at small sizes.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Bash was denied, so I couldn't run the crop script. I judged icon stroke weights by eye from the full 1280×800 image. To confirm that the six outline icons share one stroke width, check them in the source files.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 10 yes, 2 no (pictures share one rendering style and level of detail; icons share one stroke weight, cap style, and corner radius)

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The page is a help-center landing page with a search bar and eight topic cards. It has no chart, no table of figures and no dashboard.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. Controls on the page are the search field, four header nav links and eight clickable topic cards.

**Findings**
1. **"Does every control look like what it does…?" and "Does every field have its own visible label… not a placeholder alone?"** These two lines are one problem: the search field (about x 360–920, y 216–264) has no magnifier icon and no submit button. Only the grey placeholder "Search for articles" says what it is for, and that text disappears as soon as the visitor starts typing. The field still reads as something you can type in, so most visitors will find it. But it is the main control on the page and it has no search signifier, and visitors who don't press Enter by habit have nothing to click. NN/g ("Placeholders in Form Fields Are Harmful", Sherwin) and Norman (signifiers, *The Design of Everyday Things*) both cover this. The subhead "Browse a topic or search the guides" sits above the field but works as an intro line, not a label. **Fix:** put a magnifier icon inside the field on the left, or add a "Search" button on its right edge, so the field shows it is a search box even while the visitor types. Marked as convention. Weight: minor.
2. **"Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them…?"** In the 800 px shown, the visitor never sees an article. The only ways forward are typing a query or picking one of eight broad categories. A help-center home usually shows the 4–6 most asked questions, or a "Popular articles" list, under the search or under the grid, so many visitors get their answer in one click. Without it, someone with a common problem ("reset my password", "where's my order") has to guess the right category first. Contact us sits only in the header, so there is no help path in the content area either. This is my own judgment, not a sourced rule: the only entry for this line (Tognazzini) is off the reading list. **Fix:** add a short list of the top questions, plus a "Still stuck? Contact us" line after the grid. If the page carries on below the fold, check whether this already exists there. Marked as taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The search field sits right under "How can we help?" in a white field on the navy band, which makes it plainly the main action on the page. No button competes with it, so the main action is never in doubt.
- The topic cards are easy to scan. Each has a plain-language title and a one-line description in the visitor's words ("Passwords, two-step sign-in, and recovery", "Track a delivery or start a return"), so the visitor picks a category by recognising it, without needing to know how the product names things inside.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the search field, nav links and cards. The cards have thin, pale borders, so a weak default focus ring would be hard to see on them; check this with a keyboard in a live browser.
- Hover state on the cards. Nothing on a card shows it can be clicked except the card shape, so a hover change matters here.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 2 no (every control looks like what it does; every field has its own visible label), 2 unsure (focus indicator, focused control not covered).
